name: Malta
description: Malta offers expats a vibrant Mediterranean lifestyle with a strong economy, a widespread use of English, and a welcoming expat community. Its strategic location and favorable tax incentives make it an attractive destination for professionals, entrepreneurs, and retirees alike.
longdescription: Expat life in Malta is characterized by a relaxed island vibe, rich history, and diverse culture, with an expat population accounting for nearly one-third of its total residents. The economy boasts steady growth, driven by thriving sectors such as tourism, finance, iGaming, and increasingly, tech industries like software development and AI. While generally known for its friendly and hospitable locals, the island's high population density can lead to noticeable traffic congestion in urban areas, and ongoing construction is a frequent part of the landscape. Despite these challenges, Malta maintains a strong sense of community and very low crime rates, enhancing the overall quality of life for its residents. The social scene is lively, with numerous festivals, cultural events, and opportunities to connect with others through cafes, restaurants, and promenades. English is widely spoken, facilitating easy integration for international newcomers.

visas.name: Nomad Residence Permit (Malta)
visas.description: Nomad Residence Permit for remote workers who want to live and work from Malta's Mediterranean shores.

visas.name: Malta Student Visa
visas.description: Malta's student visa for non-EU/EEA nationals enrolled in a full-time recognised study programme in Malta for more than 90 days, with the right to work part-time during studies.

visas.name: Malta Family Reunification Permit
visas.description: Malta's family reunification permit allows non-EU spouses and minor dependent children of non-EU residents legally living in Malta to join them in Malta for long-term residence.

visas.name: Malta Self-Employment Permit
visas.description: Malta's self-employment permit allows non-EU nationals to establish and run their own business in Malta, an English-speaking EU member with a business-friendly regulatory environment.
benefits: Run your own business in Malta

visas.name: Malta Permanent Residence Programme (MPRP)
visas.description: Malta's Permanent Residence Programme (MPRP) grants non-EU investors permanent residency through a qualifying property purchase/rental and government contribution, offering Schengen Area access.

Citizenship by Descent.desc: Maltese citizenship by descent is available to individuals with a Maltese parent or grandparent who had citizenship by birth. If born between September 21, 1964, and July 31, 1989, citizenship may be automatic if your father was a citizen. For those born on or after August 1, 1989, citizenship is granted if at the time of birth, at least one parent was a citizen or was born in Malta. Amendments in 2007 allow second and subsequent generations born abroad to apply for citizenship by registration if a direct-line ancestor was alive on August 1, 2007, and had acquired Maltese citizenship. Applicants must provide extensive documentation, including birth and marriage certificates for each generation to prove direct lineage. Malta allows dual nationality.

Naturalization.desc: Foreigners may naturalize as Maltese citizens after residing in the country for at least four of the previous seven years, including 12 months of continuous residence immediately prior to application. Applicants must demonstrate proficiency in Maltese or English and fulfill a good character requirement. General naturalization can be a lengthy process, typically taking 5 to 18 years, suitable for those who already live in Malta long-term and do not intend to leave for extended periods. Individuals domiciled in Malta with a grandfather and great-grandfather born in Malta may naturalize with no minimum residence period. Stateless persons born in Malta may naturalize after five years of ordinary residence, while those born abroad with at least one Maltese parent may naturalize after three years of residence.

Birthright.desc: Between September 21, 1964, and August 1, 1989, all persons born in Malta automatically received citizenship at birth, regardless of their parents' nationalities. On or after August 1, 1989, individuals born in Malta receive Maltese citizenship at birth if at least one parent is a citizen or was also born in Malta.

Spouse and Family.desc: Non-citizens married to Maltese citizens can acquire citizenship by registration after five years of marriage and cohabitation. The granting of citizenship is subject to the Minister's satisfaction that it is not contrary to public interest. The five-year waiting period was introduced in 2000 to address concerns over marriages of convenience.

tax_advice:
*   **Corporate Income Tax:** Companies are subject to a flat rate of 35%, though an effective tax rate of 5% can be achieved through a full imputation system and refundable tax credits.
*   **Personal Income Tax:** Progressive rates range from 0% to a maximum of 35%. Individuals with an annual employment income lower than EUR 11,620 are not subject to tax as of January 1, 2024.
*   **Special Tax Schemes:**
    *   **Highly Qualified Persons (HQP) Rules:** Expats in senior positions in specific sectors (e.g., finance, aviation, gaming) with a minimum annual salary of €98,436 (in 2024) may benefit from a flat tax rate of 15% for a determined number of years.
    *   **Nomad Residence Permit Holders:** Digital nomads with a valid permit can qualify for a reduced income tax rate of 10% on income derived from "authorised work" as of January 1, 2024.
    *   **Permanent Resident Scheme (PRS) for Retirees:** Retiring expats pay a flat 15% tax rate on income sourced from Malta, with foreign income and capital gains being tax-exempt. A minimum annual tax of €15,000 applies.
*   **Non-Domiciled Residents:** Individuals who are resident but not domiciled in Malta are taxed on Maltese-sourced income and capital gains, as well as foreign income received in Malta; foreign capital gains are excluded from taxation.
*   **Value Added Tax (VAT):** The standard VAT rate in Malta is 18%. Reduced rates of 12%, 7%, and 5% apply to specific goods and services, such as certain human body care services, securities management, accommodation, and electricity. Zero-rated supplies include essential food, pharmaceutical products, and public transport.
*   **Double Taxation Relief:** Malta has an extensive network of double taxation treaties, which can impact tax obligations and rates.
*   **Withholding Tax:** Generally, there are no withholding taxes on outbound payments of dividends, interest, and royalties.
local_tips:
*   **Cost of Living:** Malta is generally more affordable than many Western European countries, the UK, and the USA, with overall costs estimated to be 20-30% lower. A single person can live comfortably on approximately €1,500–€2,000 per month, excluding rent.
*   **Housing:** Accommodation is a significant expense, especially in popular areas like Sliema, St. Julian's, and Valletta. A one-bedroom apartment in these areas can range from €800 to €1,200 per month, while less densely populated areas might be €1,000 to €1,500. Renting is common for newcomers, with opportunities to buy new builds.
*   **Groceries & Utilities:** Monthly grocery expenses can be around $500. Utilities typically cost between $80 and $150 per month.
*   **Language:** Both Maltese and English are official languages. English is very widely spoken (by nearly 90% of the population) and is used in business, education, and government, making it easy for expats to navigate daily life without speaking Maltese. Learning a few Maltese phrases is appreciated by locals.
*   **Safety:** Malta is considered one of the safest countries in Europe with low crime rates. Petty theft, such as pickpocketing, can occur in crowded tourist areas like Paceville and St. Julian's, so general awareness is advised.
*   **Registration:** EU/EEA/Swiss citizens intending to reside for more than three months must register with Identita (Malta's identity and immigration authority) and obtain an eResidence Card. The application is submitted online via the Expatriates Portal, followed by a biometric appointment. Non-EU nationals generally apply for a Single Permit, which covers both work and residence. It's recommended to apply within three months of arrival.
